newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Prodi saves Albania force but risks govt.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Prodi saves Albania force but risks govt.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi secured support in parliament on Wednesday to send an Italian-led security force to Albania but at the cost of a damaging rift with his hard left allies that has put his future on the line.

Prodi, facing the stiffest political challenge in 11 months in office, staved off an immediate government crisis when the centre-right opposition Freedom Alliance said it would vote with his centre-left coalition on a joint motion to deploy the force.

But it exacted a high price for voting with the government, forcing Prodi into a humiliating admission that he was not able to muster a majority of his own on the policy after key ally Communist Refoundation broke ranks and said it would vote "no".

The vote in the Chamber of Deputies (lower house) was scheduled for around 1800 GMT and was certain to result in overwhelming support for the 6,000-strong multinational force, the first of its kind to be led by Italy.
"There is a vast consensus for this mission in parliament and in the country. All the conditions are there for the mission to succeed," Prodi said in a speech replying to the debate.

Political sources said he was expected to go immediately after the vote to see President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro and inform him that his parliamentary majority had crumbled on the issue as a result of the Refoundation mutiny.

Options open to Scalfaro, the supreme arbiter in Italian politics, include asking Prodi to tender his resignation or, more likely, sending him to parliament for a confidence vote to determine whether his government stands or falls.
Prodi cannot muster a majority in the lower house without Refoundation, whose 34 deputies hold the balance of power.

The split on Albania has highlighted the vulnerability of his coalition to Refoundation's casting votes on a difficult domestic agenda, including a drive to reform the welfare state to prepare Italy for Europe's planned single currency.
Coalition parties now want a thorough review of the alliance to assess whether the hard left can be brought into line on key economic policies.

"What we have to do now is seek a confidence vote on the government's programme. The vote must be on precise issues and not general matters," said Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini, leader of the centrist Italian Renewal party.
Refoundation has said it will back Prodi on a confidence vote but party chairman Armando Cossutta appeared on Wednesday to lay down terms, signalling a potentially rocky ride ahead.

"If Prodi wants (to win) the confidence motion, then he should not enter into details," Cossutta told reporters. "If we back the motion then we will vote for it with open hearts. If not then we will vote against," he added.

The opposition supports the Albania force but, sensing an opportunity to embarrass the premier, had insisted that Prodi acknowledge that his parliamentary majority had been cut to shreds on the issue.

Prodi took steps to meet the demand in his speech opening Wednesday's debate, noting that a Refoundation "no" vote in the Senate on Tuesday, when the government's own majority was enough to get its motion through, had shown he had problems.

"I declare now that if the dissent expressed by the Communist Refoundation group persists, I will go immediately to the head of state to inform him officially of the situation and await his evaluation," Prodi said.
Maurizio Gasparri, of the hard-right National Alliance, said the turmoil demonstrated that the government was "brain dead".
"You are making the country look ridiculous. You cannot pretend that your majority hasn't dissolved," he said.

Refoundation regards the Albania force as a neo-colonialist venture and says Italian soldiers will face unacceptable risks. The mission coincides with the 58th anniversary this week of the occupation of the country by pre-war Fascist Italy.
